subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.activity_title: Playing and Thinking Through the NIM Game

tasks_in_class.description: Play the two-player NIM game: each player alternately chooses 1 or 2 to add to the running total; first to reach 10 wins. Play for a few rounds.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Can you win the game if (a)(b)(c), p.149
tasks_in_class.description: Can you win if: (a) opponent reached 6, (b) opponent reached 7, (c) opponent reached 8 and it is your turn? Who wins in each case?
Play the game with target numbers 10, 11, or 12. Find a number in each case at which you are sure you can win.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the NIM game rules: two players alternately add 1 or 2, first to reach 10 wins. Pairs play NIM Game, p.149 ("play two-player NIM game: alternately choose 1 or 2....") for several rounds, recording each running total on a scrap of paper.

Class pauses play. Groups of four work on Can you win the game if (a)(b)(c), p.149 ("can you win if opponent reached 6, 7, 8...."), reasoning backwards from the target to decide who holds the advantage at each position.

Pairs take up NIM Game extension, p.150 ("play with target numbers 10, 11, or 12...."), testing different targets and identifying a safe position. Pairs share their winning number with the class and discuss why it works.

periods.teacher_notes: Encourage students to notice that whoever controls the position 9 (one step from target) wins, then to ask what position guarantees reaching 9 — working backward in steps of 3. A common error is for students to add 1 or 2 without planning ahead; nudge them with 'What does your opponent need to be at for you to win?'
materials: Scrap paper for recording running totals

section_titles: Addition Chart — Patterns in a Table
periods.activity_title: Hunting for Patterns Inside the Addition Table

tasks_in_class.description: Identify some patterns in the addition table.
Observe where the number 9 appears in the table. How many times? What about other numbers?
Are there any rows or columns containing only even or only odd numbers? Explain your observation.
Red window frame: find row sums, column sums, diagonal sums; move frame to other places and compare. What do you notice?

homework.description: Identify patterns and relationships among numbers in the blue window frame.

time_bands.activity: Students open the 13×13 addition chart in the textbook. Working individually, they spend a quiet moment scanning the table before tackling Let Us Do Q1, p.150 ("identify some patterns in the addition table") and jotting two or three observations.

Pairs work on Let Us Do Q2, p.150 ("observe where 9 appears in the table, how many times....") and Let Us Do Q3, p.150 ("are there rows or columns with only even or only odd numbers...."), then share findings with an adjacent pair.

Groups of four use a cut-out 2×2 frame or simply mark a frame with a finger and work through Let Us Do Q4(a)(b)(c)(d), p.151 ("red window frame: find row sums, column sums, diagonal sums...."), moving the frame to at least three positions and comparing results. Groups report their finding to the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The key discovery in Q4 is that within any 2×2 window the two row sums are equal, the two column sums are equal, and the two diagonal sums are equal. Students sometimes compute each cell individually; nudge them to look at the structure — how do the four cells relate? Let Us Do Q5 on the blue window extends this and is well-suited as an at-home exploration.
materials: Textbook open to addition chart pp.150–151
Scissors and scrap paper (optional, for a moveable frame)

section_titles: Reverse and Add — Digit Patterns and Sequences
periods.activity_title: Reversing Digits and Filling Number Sequences

tasks_in_class.description: Take a 2-digit number (e.g. 27), reverse its digits (72), add them (99). Repeat for different 2-digit numbers.
What sums can we get when we add a 2-digit number with its reverse?
List all numbers which when added to their reverse give: (i) 55, (ii) 88.
Can we get a 3-digit sum? What is the smallest 3-digit sum that we can get?
Number sequence on trees counting by 50 (2540, 2590, …); fill in the missing values.
Number line with kangaroo: fill missing values at equal intervals between 7645 and beyond 7745.

homework.description: Number sequence on arches counting by 1000 (354, 1354, …); fill in the missing values.

time_bands.activity: Each student picks two or three 2-digit numbers, works through Reverse and Add (a), p.151 ("take a 2-digit number, reverse its digits, add them...."), and writes results on the board. The class collects a list of all sums obtained.

Working in pairs, students tackle Reverse and Add (b), p.151 ("what sums can we get when we add a 2-digit number with its reverse...."), then Reverse and Add (c), p.151 ("list all numbers giving 55; giving 88...."), and Reverse and Add (d), p.151 ("can we get a 3-digit sum...."). Pairs share answers; the class discusses why all sums are multiples of 11.

Individually, students fill in Fill in the blanks (a), p.151 ("number sequence on trees counting by 50....") and Fill in the blanks (c), p.151 ("number line with kangaroo: fill missing values...."). Two or three students write their answers on the board for a quick whole-class check.

periods.teacher_notes: A common difficulty is that students try random numbers for parts (b)–(d) rather than thinking about what multiples of 11 are possible; ask 'Is 11 a factor of your sum each time?' to anchor the pattern. Fill in the blanks (b) counting by 1000 makes excellent homework as the skip-counting step is large and students benefit from working at their own pace.
materials: Board or chart for collecting the class list of sums

section_titles: How Many Animals? — 4-Digit Addition with Regrouping
periods.activity_title: Building 4-Digit Addition with Blocks and Wildlife Data

tasks_in_class.description: Karnataka has 6049 elephants and Kerala has 3054. How many elephants in total? Estimate the answer first.
Gujarat 1355, Karnataka 1131, Madhya Pradesh 1817 leopards. How many total? Estimate first.

homework.description: Maharashtra has 444 tigers; MP has 341 more, Uttarakhand has 116 more. Find: (a) MP tigers, (b) UK tigers, (c) MP+UK total, (d) all three states total.

time_bands.activity: Using the Dienes block tokens shown in the textbook (or substitute counters for 1000, 100, 10, 1), model how 10 ones become 1 ten and 10 hundreds become 1 thousand with a quick concrete demonstration on the board, tying the exchange directly to the H-T-O-Th column headings.

Students read How Many Animals? Q1, p.152 ("Karnataka 6049 elephants, Kerala 3054, how many total? estimate first...."), write a quick estimate by rounding, then solve in column form. The class checks the worked example in the textbook and discusses where regrouping occurred.

Groups of three work on How Many Animals? Q2, p.153 ("Gujarat 1355, Karnataka 1131, MP 1817 leopards, total?...."), each student writing the column algorithm independently. Groups compare answers and identify any regrouping step that caused errors.

periods.teacher_notes: Regrouping across two places (ones → tens, then tens → hundreds) is the main difficulty; students often forget to carry a second time when the hundreds column also overflows. Encourage students to circle the carry digit as they write it. How Many Animals? Q3 is a multi-step chain best explored as homework so students can work through each sub-question at their own pace.

section_titles: How Many Animals? — 4-Digit Addition with Regrouping
More or Less? — 4-Digit Subtraction with Regrouping
periods.activity_title: From Tigers to Elephants: Completing Addition and Starting Subtraction

tasks_in_class.description: Maharashtra has 444 tigers; MP has 341 more, Uttarakhand has 116 more. Find: (a) MP tigers, (b) UK tigers, (c) MP+UK total, (d) all three states total.
Assam has 5719 elephants, 3965 more than Meghalaya. How many elephants are in Meghalaya? Estimate first.

time_bands.activity: Students work through How Many Animals? Q3(a)(b)(c)(d), p.154 ("Maharashtra 444 tigers; MP 341 more, Uttarakhand 116 more — find each state count and the grand total...."), writing each sub-question as a separate column addition. The class discusses the multi-step chain on the board, checking each intermediate result.

Introduce subtraction with regrouping using the block exchange shown in the textbook: 1 hundred is traded for 10 tens, 1 thousand for 10 hundreds. Demonstrate with a brief board example before moving to the wildlife context.

Students read More or Less? Q1, p.155 ("Assam has 5719 elephants, 3965 more than Meghalaya — how many in Meghalaya? estimate first...."), write a rounding estimate, then solve in column form. A volunteer writes the working on the board and the class identifies the regrouping steps.

periods.teacher_notes: The shift from addition to subtraction regrouping is the unit's conceptual hinge; emphasise that 'borrowing' is the inverse of 'carrying' — students exchange a larger unit for 10 smaller ones rather than bundling up. A frequent error is subtracting the top digit from the bottom when the bottom is larger; asking 'Can I take 6 tens from 1 ten without trading?' redirects thinking.

section_titles: More or Less? — 4-Digit Subtraction with Regrouping
periods.activity_title: Subtracting Animals and Mapping Our Results

tasks_in_class.description: 2022 leopard count in Central India and Eastern Ghats is 8820, up 749 from 2018. How many leopards were there in 2018? Estimate first.
Write the number of animals on the India map using data from previous problems (elephants, tigers, leopards by state/region).

time_bands.activity: Students solve More or Less? Q2, p.155–156 ("2022 leopard count 8820, up 749 from 2018 — how many in 2018? estimate first....") individually, showing the estimate and the column algorithm. The class checks and discusses the regrouping — particularly the zero in the tens place of the minuend.

Students turn to the India map on p.156 for the Map activity, p.156 ("write number of animals on the India map using data from previous problems...."). They locate each relevant state, recall the animal counts from their notebooks, and write the figures on the map. Pairs cross-check each other's entries.

periods.teacher_notes: Q2 involves 8820 − 749, where the tens digit of the minuend is 2; students need to regroup twice in sequence. The map task consolidates all computed values from the addition and subtraction work on wildlife data and gives students a geographic picture of India's animal populations — a meaningful payoff for the column-arithmetic work done so far.
materials: Pencils and coloured pencils (optional, for the map)

section_titles: Let Us Do — Mixed Word Problems and Money
periods.activity_title: Visitors, Juice, and Vehicles: Applying Addition and Subtraction

tasks_in_class.description: Kaziranga: Dec 8591, Nov 6415 visitors. (a) How many more in Dec than Nov? (b) Nov is 1587 more than Oct; find Oct visitors.
Juice factory: pineapple 1348, passion fruit 4781. (a) Guava = pineapple + 759. (b) Orange = guava + 1257. (c) Is guava + orange more or less than passion fruit?
Solve 10 addition and subtraction problems: e.g. 1459+476, 3863+4188, 7293−2819, 8006−5567 (4-digit).

homework.description: Vehicles: jeeps 6304. (a) Buses = jeeps + 253. (b) Tractors = buses − 5247. (c) Taxis = tractors + 1579. (d) Arrange vehicle counts lowest to highest.

time_bands.activity: Students solve Let Us Do Q1(a)(b), p.157 ("Kaziranga Dec 8591, Nov 6415 visitors; more in Dec than Nov? and find Oct....") working individually, then compare with a partner. Both parts require choosing between addition and subtraction, so a brief class discussion on choosing the operation is worthwhile.

Groups of three work through Let Us Do Q2(a)(b)(c), p.157–158 ("juice factory: guava = pineapple + 759; orange = guava + 1257; compare guava + orange with passion fruit...."), building each answer from the previous one. Part (c) invites comparison without a further calculation, prompting estimation.

Students work individually on a selection from Let Us Do Q4(a)–(j), p.158 ("solve 10 addition and subtraction problems: e.g. 1459+476, 7293−2819...."), completing as many as time allows. The teacher circulates, noting which regrouping scenarios cause errors.

periods.teacher_notes: Multi-step chains like Q2 and Q3 often lead students to carry a wrong intermediate answer forward; encourage them to box each sub-answer before using it in the next step. Let Us Do Q3 on vehicles is assigned as homework because it extends the chain to four steps, giving students room to work at a careful pace.

section_titles: Let Us Do — Mixed Word Problems and Money
Let Us Solve — Column Algorithm Practice
periods.activity_title: Deposit Slips and Column Drill: Deepening the Algorithm

tasks_in_class.description: Baal Mela: help Raju (₹2045), Rani (₹3578), Roja (₹1240) fill deposit slips with possible combinations of notes (500, 100, 50, 10) and coins (5, 2, 1).

time_bands.activity: Groups of three work through Let Us Do Q5, p.159–160 ("Baal Mela: fill deposit slips for Raju ₹2045, Rani ₹3578, Roja ₹1240 using notes and coins...."). Each group finds one valid combination per person. Groups then share different solutions, noticing that multiple decompositions are possible for the same amount.

Students complete Let Us Solve Q1(a)(b)(c)(d), p.161 ("solve 4 column-format problems: 3695+4208; 2507+6847; 6352−3521; 8803−5726....") in their notebooks. The class checks answers together on the board, with students explaining each regrouping step aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: The deposit-slip task develops place-value understanding in a monetary context — decomposing ₹3578 into 500s, 100s, 50s, 10s, and coins mirrors the Th-H-T-O structure students have used in column work. In Q1(d), 8803 − 5726 involves a zero in the tens column of the minuend and is the most challenging regrouping scenario of the set; address it carefully if several students struggle.
materials: Play money (notes and coins) or printed denomination cards

section_titles: Let Us Solve — Column Algorithm Practice
Let Us Solve — Mental Strategies and Reasoning
periods.activity_title: Arranging in Columns, Then Finding the Easy Way

tasks_in_class.description: Find easy ways to solve 9 problems (e.g. 8787−99, 4596+104, 3999+290). Share thinking with the class.
Use <, =, > to compare 4 expression pairs without calculating (e.g. 54+97 vs 54+90; 73−54 vs 73−56). Reason and share.

time_bands.activity: Students arrange and solve a selection of Let Us Solve Q2(a)–(h), p.161 ("arrange in columns: 3683−971, 8432−46, 4011−3666, 5203−2745...."), focusing especially on problems where the number being subtracted has fewer digits (8432 − 46), ensuring correct column alignment.

The class works on Let Us Solve Q1(a)–(i), p.162 ("find easy ways to solve e.g. 8787−99, 4596+104, 3999+290...."). Students try each problem mentally, then share their shortcut strategy. Different approaches (subtract 100 add 1; add 100 subtract 4) are listed on the board.

Pairs work through Let Us Solve Q2, p.162 ("use <, =, > to compare expression pairs without calculating: 54+97 vs 54+90; 73−54 vs 73−56...."), writing reasoning in words. Two pairs share their reasoning with the class, demonstrating that comparison is possible without full computation.

periods.teacher_notes: In Q2(a)–(h), problems like 8432 − 46 and 3567 + 77 trip students who misalign digits to the left rather than the right; emphasise right-alignment in the column. The mental strategies in Q1 build the important insight that adjusting one number and compensating in the other preserves the result — a foundation for flexible computation.

section_titles: Let Us Solve — Mental Strategies and Reasoning
periods.activity_title: Derived Facts, Computation Fluency, and the Grid Puzzle

tasks_in_class.description: Fill a 3×3 grid with numbers 1–9 so the difference between any two neighbouring squares (connected by a line) is odd. Find other ways. Can you make all differences even?

time_bands.activity: Students work through Let Us Solve Q3, p.162 ("use given equations to find derived values: 139+175=314 → 314−175=?; 354+167=521 → 354+168=?...."), writing the reasoning — what changes by how much — next to each answer. Pairs compare and discuss.

Students complete Add Q1(a)–(j), p.163 ("solve 10 addition problems: e.g. 2783+378, 8948+97, 4999+3888....") individually in column form, using mental shortcuts where they can. A quick show of hands identifies which problems caused regrouping across two places.

Groups of three take on Fill the squares Q3, p.163 ("fill a 3×3 grid with 1–9 so every neighbouring pair differs by an odd amount...."), trying several arrangements and then asking whether an all-even version is possible. Groups share one working arrangement and their answer to the even-difference question.

periods.teacher_notes: Q3's derived-facts work helps students see that addition and subtraction are inverse operations and that changing one addend by 1 changes the sum by 1. The grid puzzle connects odd-even parity to subtraction: the difference of two numbers is odd only when one is odd and the other is even, so placing numbers so every adjacent pair has mixed parity is the underlying constraint. Subtract Q2(a)–(j) is assigned as homework to consolidate subtraction fluency.
materials: Scrap paper for grid puzzle trials

items.prompt: Two players are playing the NIM game. They take turns adding 1 or 2 to a running total. The player who reaches 10 wins. The running total is now at 7 and it is your turn. Which number should you add to be sure you win?

options.label: D
options.text: Either 1 or 2 — your opponent cannot reach 10 on their next turn no matter what they add

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Add either 1 (total 8) or 2 (total 9). If you reach 8, your opponent adds 1 or 2 (total 9 or 10). If total is 9, opponent must add 1 or 2, reaching 10 or 11 — but reaching 10 means opponent wins. Re-examining: at total 7 (your turn), adding 3 is not allowed. Adding 2 gives 9; opponent must then add 1 or 2, reaching 10 or 11. Reaching 10 means opponent wins. Adding 1 gives 8; opponent adds 1 (=9) or 2 (=10). If opponent reaches 10, opponent wins. The winning position is to reach 9 on your turn so opponent must overshoot. At total 7, add 2 to reach 9; opponent must add 1 or 2 to get 10 or 11, but only 10 wins and opponent does reach 10 by adding 1. Therefore the safe move is to reach 9 — add 2. Answer: Add 2 to make the total 9.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Work backwards from the target: whoever reaches 9 forces the opponent to reach 10 on the opponent's own next turn.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Adds 1 to reach 8, leaving the opponent able to reach 9 and then control the game — does not reason about the opponent's response.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Tries to add 3, which is not a permitted move in the game — misremembers the rules.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Believes any move wins from position 7 without reasoning about what the opponent can do next.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student act out both choices with a partner using counters; stretch: ask what number you must reach to guarantee a win when the target is 12.

exercise.description: Play the two-player NIM game: each player alternately chooses 1 or 2 to add to the running total; first to reach 10 wins. Play for a few rounds.

items.section_title: Reverse and Add — Digit Patterns and Sequences
items.prompt: Take the number 34. Reverse its digits to get 43. Add the two numbers. Now take the number 52, reverse it to get 25, and add. Write both sums. What do you notice about these sums?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 34 + 43 = 77; 52 + 25 = 77. Both sums are 77. (Any two 2-digit numbers with digit sum equal are accepted; the key observation is that both results are multiples of 11.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the original and reversed number in columns, then check whether the result is a multiple of 11.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use the column algorithm step by step for each addition; stretch: ask the student to pick a third pair and predict the sum before computing.

exercise.description: Take a 2-digit number (e.g. 27), reverse its digits (72), add them (99). Repeat for different 2-digit numbers.

items.prompt: In the NIM game (target 10, add 1 or 2 each turn), the running total is at 6 and it is your turn. Explain whether you can be sure of winning, and what you should add.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes. Add 1 to make the total 7. Then whatever your opponent adds (1 or 2), the total becomes 8 or 9. If 8, you add 2 to reach 10 and win. If 9, you add 1 to reach 10 and win. So adding 1 from position 6 guarantees a win.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Work backwards: identify positions 7 and 9 as safe positions that force a win, then choose the move that puts the total at 7.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student play out the possibilities with a partner using a number line marked 0–10; stretch: ask which starting positions from 1–9 guarantee a win for the player whose turn it is.

exercise.book_ref: Can you win the game if (a)(b)(c), p.149
exercise.description: Can you win if: (a) opponent reached 6, (b) opponent reached 7, (c) opponent reached 8 and it is your turn? Who wins in each case?

items.section_title: Addition Chart — Patterns in a Table
items.prompt: Look at this 2×2 window taken from an addition table. The four numbers in the window are 7, 8, 8, and 9. Find the row sums and the column sums. What do you notice? Will this pattern hold if you move the window to a different position in the table?
items.visual_stimulus:
| + | col A | col B |
| row 1 | 7 | 8 |
| row 2 | 8 | 9 |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 1 sum = 7 + 8 = 15. Row 2 sum = 8 + 9 = 17. Column 1 sum = 7 + 8 = 15. Column 2 sum = 8 + 9 = 17. Row sums equal the column sums of the same pair. In any 2×2 window from the addition table, the two row sums are equal to the two column sums respectively, and this pattern holds wherever the window is placed.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add each row and each column of the 2×2 window and compare the totals.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student compute each sum one at a time and circle matching results; stretch: ask the student to explain why neighbouring cells in the addition table always differ by exactly 1.

exercise.description: Red window frame: find row sums, column sums, diagonal sums; move frame to other places and compare. What do you notice?

items.section_title: Reverse and Add — Digit Patterns and Sequences
items.prompt: A student adds a 2-digit number to the number formed by reversing its digits. Which of the following could be the sum?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 66. When any 2-digit number is added to its digit-reversal, the result is always a multiple of 11. Among the options, only 66 = 11 × 6 is a multiple of 11.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check each option for divisibility by 11; only a multiple of 11 can be a reverse-and-add sum.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Chooses 45, which is a multiple of 9 but not 11 — confuses the reverse-and-add pattern with the digit-sum divisibility rule for 9.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Chooses 70, a round number — guesses without applying the multiple-of-11 constraint.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Chooses 83, an odd non-multiple of 11 — does not recognise that all reverse-and-add sums are multiples of 11.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to try one example (e.g. 23 + 32) and check which option their sum matches; stretch: ask the student to list all multiples of 11 between 11 and 99 and explain which ones are possible reverse-and-add sums.

exercise.description: What sums can we get when we add a 2-digit number with its reverse?

items.section_title: Reverse and Add — Digit Patterns and Sequences
items.prompt: A student claims: 'I can find a 2-digit number whose reverse-and-add sum is a 3-digit number.' Is the student right? If yes, give an example. If no, explain why not.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes. The largest reverse-and-add sum comes from a number with the largest possible digit total, such as 99: 99 + 99 = 198, which is a 3-digit number. Another example: 91 + 19 = 110. The smallest 3-digit sum is 110 (from 91 + 19 or 19 + 91).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Try the largest digit-sum 2-digit numbers (where both digits are large) and check whether the result exceeds 99.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to add 91 and 19 in columns to see whether the result has three digits; stretch: ask the student to find all 2-digit numbers whose reverse-and-add sum is exactly 110.

exercise.description: Can we get a 3-digit sum? What is the smallest 3-digit sum that we can get?

items.section_title: Let Us Do — Mixed Word Problems and Money
items.prompt: Meena wants to deposit ₹1025 at a bank. She has notes of ₹500, ₹100, and ₹50, and coins of ₹5. Write one way she could make exactly ₹1025 using these denominations.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One valid answer: 2 × ₹500 = ₹1000, 0 × ₹100, 1 × ₹50 = ₹50 would give ₹1050 (too much). Correct: 2 × ₹500 = ₹1000; then ₹25 remaining = 0 × ₹100 + 0 × ₹50 + 5 × ₹5 = ₹25. Total: ₹1025. Another valid answer: 1 × ₹500 + 5 × ₹100 + 0 × ₹50 + 5 × ₹5 = ₹500 + ₹500 + ₹25 = ₹1025. Accept any correct combination.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Start with the largest denomination that fits, subtract from the total, and repeat for smaller denominations until the amount is reached.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a table with denomination columns and ask the student to fill in how many of each; stretch: ask the student to find a second different combination that also totals ₹1025.

exercise.description: Baal Mela: help Raju (₹2045), Rani (₹3578), Roja (₹1240) fill deposit slips with possible combinations of notes (500, 100, 50, 10) and coins (5, 2, 1).

items.section_title: Let Us Solve — Mental Strategies and Reasoning
items.prompt: Without calculating, which sign correctly completes this statement: 63 + 84 __ 63 + 80?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 63 + 84 > 63 + 80, because 84 is greater than 80 and both are added to the same number 63, so the sum with 84 must be larger.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the second addends: since 84 > 80 and the first addend is the same, the expression with the larger second addend gives the larger sum.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Chooses = — may believe the same first number makes both sums equal, ignoring the different second addends.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Chooses < — reverses the relationship, possibly misreading which side has the larger addend.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Thinks full calculation is needed — does not apply addend-comparison reasoning.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to imagine adding 4 more sweets to one bag — which bag ends up heavier; stretch: create a similar comparison with subtraction (e.g. 73 − 45 vs 73 − 40) and reason through it.

exercise.description: Use <, =, > to compare 4 expression pairs without calculating (e.g. 54+97 vs 54+90; 73−54 vs 73−56). Reason and share.

items.section_title: Let Us Solve — Mental Strategies and Reasoning
items.prompt: You are told that 246 + 138 = 384. Using only this fact (without recalculating), write the answers to: (a) 384 − 138 = ? and (b) 246 + 139 = ?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) 384 − 138 = 246, because subtraction undoes addition. (b) 246 + 139 = 385, because 139 is one more than 138, so the sum is one more than 384.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the inverse relationship for (a), and the effect of increasing one addend by 1 for (b).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a simple number bond diagram showing 246, 138, and 384; stretch: ask what 247 + 138 equals using the same given fact.

items.section_title: Reverse and Add — Digit Patterns and Sequences
items.prompt: A number sequence counts on by 50 each time. The first number is 3410. What is the fourth number in the sequence?

what_each_option_reveals.B: Gives 3550 — may have added 50 only twice (3410 + 140 = 3550 is wrong, or confused number of steps).
what_each_option_reveals.A: Gives 3460 — stops after one skip, finding only the second term instead of the fourth.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Gives 3610 — adds 50 four times instead of three, counting the starting number as a step.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw four boxes and fill the first (3410), then add 50 step by step; stretch: ask what the tenth number in the sequence would be.

exercise.description: Number sequence on trees counting by 50 (2540, 2590, …); fill in the missing values.

items.section_title: Reverse and Add — Digit Patterns and Sequences
items.prompt: A kangaroo hops along a number line, making equal jumps. It lands on 5320 and then on 5345. What is the size of each jump? Fill in the missing number the kangaroo would land on after two more jumps from 5345.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each jump = 5345 − 5320 = 25. Two more jumps: 5345 + 25 = 5370, then 5370 + 25 = 5395. The missing numbers are 5370 and 5395.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the interval by subtracting the first value from the second, then add that interval twice.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: mark the two given points on a drawn number line and count the gap; stretch: ask what number the kangaroo would land on after five more jumps from 5395.

exercise.description: Number line with kangaroo: fill missing values at equal intervals between 7645 and beyond 7745.

items.section_title: More or Less? — 4-Digit Subtraction with Regrouping
items.prompt: A wildlife reserve counted 7240 animals in 2022 and 6483 animals in 2023. How many fewer animals were counted in 2023?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract using the column algorithm with regrouping: regroup the tens column (4 tens → 3 tens 10 ones; still insufficient in ones, so regroup hundreds as well).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the subtraction in column form and ask the student to identify which column needs regrouping first; stretch: ask the student to verify by adding 6483 + 757 to check it equals 7240.

exercise.description: Write the number of animals on the India map using data from previous problems (elephants, tigers, leopards by state/region).

items.section_title: Let Us Solve — Column Algorithm Practice

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add in columns right to left: 6+5=11 (write 1, carry 1); 3+9+1=13 (write 3, carry 1); 7+8+1=16 (write 6, carry 1); 4+2+1=7. Result: 7631.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a pre-drawn Th-H-T-O column grid for the student to fill in; stretch: ask the student to estimate first by rounding to the nearest hundred, then check how close the estimate is.

items.section_title: Let Us Solve — Mental Strategies and Reasoning

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add in columns right to left: 8+3=11 (write 1, carry 1); 4+5+1=10 (write 0, carry 1); 6+9+1=16 (write 6, carry 1); 3+4+1=8. Result: 8601.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: work through the ones column together, circling the carry digit before moving to the next column; stretch: ask the student to use a mental strategy (e.g. 3648 + 5000 − 47) and check it matches the column answer.

items.section_title: How Many Animals? — 4-Digit Addition with Regrouping
items.prompt: A forest in Rajasthan has 2748 deer and a forest in Uttar Pradesh has 4365 deer. How many deer are there in both forests together?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2748 + 4365 = 7113. There are 7113 deer in both forests together.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add in columns with regrouping: 8+5=13 (write 3, carry 1); 4+6+1=11 (write 1, carry 1); 7+3+1=11 (write 1, carry 1); 2+4+1=7. Result: 7113.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the Th-H-T-O columns and work one column at a time, circling carries; stretch: ask the student to estimate by rounding each number to the nearest thousand and compare with the exact answer.

exercise.description: Karnataka has 6049 elephants and Kerala has 3054. How many elephants in total? Estimate the answer first.

items.section_title: How Many Animals? — 4-Digit Addition with Regrouping
items.prompt: A state has 512 rhinos. A neighbouring state has 234 more rhinos than the first state. A third state has 189 more rhinos than the second state. How many rhinos does the third state have?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Second state: 512 + 234 = 746. Third state: 746 + 189 = 935. The third state has 935 rhinos.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Solve as a two-step addition chain: find the second state's count, then add the given extra to find the third state's count.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a step-by-step arrow diagram showing State 1 → State 2 → State 3 with the additions labelled; stretch: ask the student to find the total rhino count across all three states.

exercise.description: Maharashtra has 444 tigers; MP has 341 more, Uttarakhand has 116 more. Find: (a) MP tigers, (b) UK tigers, (c) MP+UK total, (d) all three states total.

items.section_title: More or Less? — 4-Digit Subtraction with Regrouping
items.prompt: A sanctuary in State A has 6312 birds. It has 2485 more birds than State B. How many birds does State B have?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract using the column algorithm with regrouping: 2−5 requires regrouping tens; 0 tens requires regrouping hundreds; continue through the columns.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to check whether 'more than' means they should add or subtract, and identify the starting number; stretch: ask the student to verify by computing 3827 + 2485 and checking it equals 6312.

exercise.description: Assam has 5719 elephants, 3965 more than Meghalaya. How many elephants are in Meghalaya? Estimate first.

items.section_title: Let Us Do — Mixed Word Problems and Money
items.prompt: A national park had 7240 visitors in March and 5863 visitors in April. How many more visitors came in March than in April?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 7240 − 5863 = 1377. There were 1377 more visitors in March.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract 5863 from 7240 using the column algorithm, regrouping the tens and hundreds as needed.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to estimate by rounding to the nearest hundred before computing; stretch: ask how many visitors came in both months combined.

exercise.description: Kaziranga: Dec 8591, Nov 6415 visitors. (a) How many more in Dec than Nov? (b) Nov is 1587 more than Oct; find Oct visitors.

items.section_title: Let Us Do — Mixed Word Problems and Money
items.prompt: A factory made 2156 bottles of mango juice. It made 843 more bottles of lemon juice than mango juice. How many bottles of lemon juice did it make? How many bottles of juice did the factory make in all?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add 843 to the mango count to find lemon, then add both counts for the total.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: break the problem into two clearly labelled steps in the notebook; stretch: ask the student to find how many more bottles of lemon juice than mango juice were made, and check it matches the given 843.

exercise.description: Juice factory: pineapple 1348, passion fruit 4781. (a) Guava = pineapple + 759. (b) Orange = guava + 1257. (c) Is guava + orange more or less than passion fruit?
